item.title: StackOverflow now gets fewer than 1000 questions a month
item.description:
Source: data.stackexchange.com

Top Comment:

What is this "Stack Overflow" you speak of?

Oh yes. Now I remember. I used to visit the site every day.

I love helping my fellow developers and answering their questions whenever I can.

My reputation there is 29,020, and I've contributed 645 quality answers.

I used to brag about this.

Now I had to think a bit to remember SO still exists.

My last answer was on May 28, 2021, over five years ago.

Obviously it wasn't LLMs that drove me away. And I'm not sure what it was.

Was it the culture, as others here pointed out? Or did I just get busy with other things?

---

Update: Now I think I remember what muted my enthusiasm.

Some of you older programmers may have used jQuery.

There is a common convention to use $ as the first character of a variable name that is a jQuery object:

  var $foo = $('#foo');
One of my few claims to fame is that I invented that convention and promoted it on the early jQuery mailing list.

Someone asked about this:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/205853/why-would-a-javas...

The top-rated answer, with 1542 votes, is a good summary.

The second answer, with 278 votes, is as irrelevant as an answer can be.

I'm in third place with 71 votes. I gave the story behind the naming convention, because I like people to know the "how and why".

It gets better! This question was marked as a duplicate of another one. That other question has a wild variety of answers, but none that does what I tried to do: explain the reason and background for the convention.

Ah well. It was fun while it lasted.

item.title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
item.description:
Source: sidbala.com

Top Comment:

Had the pleasure of working with Jason Garrett-Glaser (better known as DarkShikari) circa 2011 on a patch for x264 to better utilize more cores (slice-threaded lookahead). At the time he was working with Sony to optimize their PlayStation game streaming service, and this had the potential to lower encoding latency (critical to game streaming) even on same-core systems by spreading the frame over more cores to do more parallel work, and doing more intelligent scheduling and convergence after that tile-based work was reconverged into a frame. At the time we were using servers with 48 physical cores to do transcoding, a bit of a rarity in a single NUMA space back then and there were no instances to test this on so I flamegraph traced a few encodes at very high thread parallel counts and send back the instrumented profiles (from a custom compiled version) showing the core work being done and he used that to optimize the motion estimation code which worked on the first shot to perfectly level out cpu usage and increase encoding speed across ~24 cores (was previously topping out around 8 and running one core hot iirc). I got a look into how exotic and complex this project was, particularly in terms how low level and advanced things like motion estimation, quantizing and perceptual compression were... it was and still is sort of magic how many smart techniques are baked into something that we barely pay attention to. They were, even at that time, working on x265.

His blog, Diary of an x264 developer, was a great read too for anyone wanting to get a vantage point on how crazy that codebase was.

[1]https://github.com/mstorsjo/x264/blob/master/doc/threads.txt

(edit: was Gaikai that was acquired by Sony in 2012 and is the basis for PlayStation Now)

item.description:

India: 47M

China: 358M

Both countries have roughly the same population. The IPv4 problem has been swept under the rug with CGNAT and a normal person doesn't even notice it. But it sucks. Forget having a dedicated IP, even on a broadband connection, you don't get a public IP that's truly yours. According to IPInfo[1], there are around 1,000 users sharing my IP. I get flagged for malicious activity, and online gaming is impossible without a Tailscale relay.

Of course, much of this comes down to the bad luck (+ policies) of developing late, when most IPv4 blocks had already been allocated. But it's pretty unfair how US DoD, Apple, Ford, and others [1] are sitting on enormous IPv4 blocks they'll probably never fully use, and may never sell. Meanwhile I am sharing a single public IP with a thousand strangers.

item.title: What we know so far about Spain train crash
item.description:
Source: www.bbc.com

Top Comment:

The following is hypothetical, since we do not have a proper safety report yet.

It sounds like the issue happened, because there was an error in the line-based train control system (LZB), which led to falling back to the point-based train control system (ASFA). However since there are more virtual blocks in LZB, than physical blocks in ASFA, this means that suddenly more than one train is in one block, which violates the most basic assumption of train control. That requires the trains to not rely on the train control at all, even if it says that the block is clear, but instead are operated manually.

I do not know what the proper procedures for that are in Spain, but in e.g. Germany that seems to require driving by sight. However that is also only after a number of accidents due this situation. So the following seem to be similar accidents from Germany:

- https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenbahnunfall_von_Meerbusch-...

- On April 9, 2002, a near-collision occurred near Fallersleben. After a computer at the LZB control center in Fallersleben crashed, two trains on each of the two main tracks came to a stop. When the computer was restarted, the rear train in each pair was signaled a speed of 160 km/h, while the front train in each pair was signaled 0 km/h. One of the two train operators following saw the train stopped in front of him; the other, as a precaution, contacted the operations center, which warned him not to proceed.

item.title: We won't "just hang out"
item.description:
Source: borretti.me

Top Comment:

I dunno—I spend a lot of time “just hanging out” with people who aren’t particularly dazzled by work or intellectual pursuits or higher education. I feel like those constitute one set of processes by which people come together and form relationships and, for those of us who are mainly familiar with that set, it can be instructive to seek out communities that form without any of those elements.

One place to look might be ministry or service. Illness, loss, grief, infirmity, death, age, family strains—people require care and people give care regardless of their postgraduate endeavors. Nuns and Jesuits and the like aren’t for everybody—but look to the neediest among us and, in large parts of the world, those sorts of order are the people doing the invisible, unglamorous, uneconomical, “chop wood, carry water” form of devotion and social labor day in and day out. In intimate community even with very difficult (and sometimes ungrateful) members.

Another might be the sort of ad hoc communities that arise in exigency: disaster, forced migration, encampments, solidarity against forces of difficulty.

Unhoused, unemployed, and retired people can provide a particularly illuminating contrast to the pastimes and concerns that animate a working life. A visible minority fill their days with addiction, but a whole lot are complete and interesting people with the full range of human ambitions and desires and fears and joys, and somehow they fill their waking hours with more than just material striving.

Another might be organizations like union halls, advocacy groups, music scenes, circus folk, jugglers, running clubs, political groups…

Kids are great for this too. They do a lot of hanging out, with nothing more than imagination and a drive to self-expression.

Even our hominid ancestors do a pretty good job of hanging out litigating social hierarchy and nurturing one another—no university degree or novel engineering task required…
